prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a clean example of a discovery that changes what can be measured and how accurately. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removed the trade-off between long interrogation of many atoms and light-shift perturbation, and Katori and Ye together took strontium lattice clocks to roughly 1e-18 fractional uncertainty, about two orders of magnitude beyond the caesium standard. The result has been reproduced and surpassed in several laboratories, it underpins the discussion of a redefinition of the second, and it supports tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy. The two-person attribution is unusually clear: Katori for the concept and first demonstrations, Ye for the systematic-uncertainty and coherence record and the many-body clock work. Four colleagues rank it in their top five, and Lindroth, whose atomic-structure expertise bears directly on magic wavelengths and blackbody shifts, ranks it first.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is overlap and the invention-versus-discovery question. The 2005 prize honoured the frequency comb and the 2012 prize honoured ion control, so some members may see lattice clocks as a refinement of recognised work, and the second has not yet been redefined, so recognition rests on demonstrated performance rather than adoption. Other lattice-clock and ion-clock groups (for example the Paris, PTB and NIST ion-clock efforts) are not in the credited set. Against B046, my preferred prize has fewer top-three placements, and a committee that weights breadth of a new field over precision of a technique could reasonably choose twisted bilayer graphene.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first because a flat-band prediction was confirmed by a decisive experiment and the field has grown enormously, while placing lattice clocks fifth and flagging overlap with the comb and ion-clock prizes.
responses.response: I accept that B046 is the best-supported candidate on the table and that the theory-plus-experiment pattern is clean, so I list it as my first alternative. My reservation is timing and credit. The central observations are from 2018, the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved, and you yourself note that Yuan Cao and other experimental groups fall outside the credited names, which makes the experimental allocation a real judgement call. On overlap I disagree with you. The comb prize concerned the measurement of optical frequencies and the lattice clock is the system that exploits that ruler, with a distinct idea (magic-wavelength trapping) and a distinct result. I would not read it as incremental.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first as a clear, original invention whose atomic-structure side (magic wavelengths, blackbody and higher-order light shifts) has lasting consequences, and notes that the comb prize already covered a different part.
responses.response: I agree, and I would add that it is the control of systematic shifts that makes this a discovery-level result and not only engineering: the 1e-18 figure exists because the shifts were understood and then suppressed. Your caution about waiting for the formal redefinition of the second is the real uncertainty. I would not wait, because the prize rests on the demonstrated performance, which independent clocks now agree on, and a redefinition would be a consequence of it, not a precondition.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks fluctuation theorems first as an original, clean idea that is now a standard tool in stochastic thermodynamics, while acknowledging that credit among Evans, Cohen, Gallavotti, Searles, Jarzynski and Crooks is contested and that some will see it as framework and not discovery.
responses.response: The conceptual quality is not in doubt, but I find your own attribution caveat decisive for this year. If the credit among six or more people is genuinely disputed and the credited list omits some of them, we cannot write a defensible two-name citation, whereas for lattice clocks the split is clear. I also share your worry that it may be read as a framework; the experimental verifications are important but largely test relations that follow from known dynamics. I would keep B030 in view for a later year once the priority question is better settled.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first for its original architecture and large impact on superconducting processors, while noting the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, the missing credit for Girvin and Huang, and his own proximity to the field.
responses.response: I value the disclosure and I take the impact seriously, but I side with your own caution on timing and attribution. Following the 2025 circuit prize so soon with a related one invites the criticism that we are rewarding a single technology twice, and the division between the 2004 proposal, the first strong-coupling experiment and the transmon and readout work is more contested than for clocks. I rank it sixth. If the committee does move on quantum information hardware, I would look first at B018, where the gap to the 2012 prize is larger.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats lattice clocks as a distinct discovery or as a continuation of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the second.
Priority details for the early magic-wavelength proposals and first lattice-clock demonstrations are from memory and unverified.
Whether a quantum-information prize on trapped ions (B018) is complicated by the missing credit for Wineland and Monroe.
statement.conflict_note: I spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory, and Jun Ye is a close scientific descendant of that JILA environment, so a committee colleague could reasonably regard this as a connection that merits disclosure for B041. It is a documented professional link to a mentor, not a collaboration with Ye or Katori, and I know of no joint work, funding or institutional tie to either. As a Lund atomic physicist with European quantum-memory collaborations, I also note proximity to the trapped-ion and cold-atom quantum-information community (B018, B038), although I am not aware of a specific relationship with Cirac, Zoller or Blatt. I would accept recusal on B041 if colleagues judge the Hall connection sufficient.
